prompt.context: Our client, Tarrant Fixtures, is a low-intensity manufacturing company that produces display fixtures for retail clients. The company's financial performance has deteriorated in each of the last three years. Specifically, they are concerned with the company's falling Return on Investment (ROI). The CEO has asked us to look into this problem.
prompt.question: How can Tarrant Fixtures get back on track?

clarifying_info.q: What types of products does Tarrant Fixtures make?
clarifying_info.a: Two types: Custom displays (50% of sales) — produced only when an order is placed and payment is received; and Standard displays (50% of sales) — manufactured to open standard sizes/types and stored in inventory (built-to-stock).

clarifying_info.q: How many standardized products are there?
clarifying_info.a: 5 standardized products account for 80% of sales in standardized products. The number of standardized products increased from 5 to 12 over the last 3 years.

clarifying_info.q: What has happened to revenues over the past three years?
clarifying_info.a: Total revenues grew by 25%, from $100M to $125M, equally across both product types.
Costs of production (COGS, labor, SG&A, etc.) have remained stable as a percentage of revenue at 80%.

clarifying_info.q: Has there been any new capital investment?
clarifying_info.a: No. The company has no new investments in Property, Plant, & Equipment (CAPEX = $0).

clarifying_info.q: What is the working capital situation?
clarifying_info.a: Total working capital employed three years ago was $80M; today it is $130M. Inventory levels have increased by 300%, from $25M to $75M (primarily in finished goods).
The market has grown at 25% over the past three years.
The client has remained the industry market share leader in displays over the past three years and has maintained 25% market share.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive environment like?
clarifying_info.a: There are several players in the market, but everything has remained stable from a competitive standpoint.

exhibits.title: Working Capital Statement
exhibits.shows: A line-by-line working capital statement showing categories of capital employed (including inventory, PP&E, accounts receivable, accounts payable, and cash) for Year 1 and Year 3.
exhibits.data: Year 1 Total Working Capital: $80M; Year 3 Total Working Capital: $130M; Inventory Year 1: $25M; Inventory Year 3: $75M; all other working capital components stable

framework: Define ROI: ROI = Net Profit / Capital Employed
Examine the numerator — Net Profit trend over 3 years
Examine the denominator — Capital Employed: break into PP&E vs. Working Capital
Within Working Capital, decompose into inventory, AR, AP, cash
Identify root cause of inventory build-up
Recommend actions to reduce inventory and restore ROI

questions.prompt: What is the formula for ROI, and what are the two components you would investigate?
questions.guidance: ROI = Net Profit / Capital Employed. A strong candidate immediately identifies both the numerator (profitability) and denominator (capital base) as potential drivers and structures the analysis around both before diving in.

questions.prompt: Has net profit been the cause of the ROI decline? Calculate net profit for Year 1 and Year 3.
questions.guidance: Net profit has NOT been the cause. Revenue grew 25% and costs held at 80% of revenue, so absolute profit also grew 25%. The numerator is not the culprit — the candidate should pivot to the denominator.

math.setup: Net Profit = Revenue × (1 − Cost%) where Cost% = 80%
steps: Change: +$5M (+25%) — profit grew in line with revenue
math.answer: Net profit grew from $20M to $25M; this is NOT the cause of ROI deterioration.

questions.prompt: Examine Capital Employed. What has changed and why has ROI fallen?
questions.guidance: PP&E is unchanged (no CAPEX). Working capital increased by $50M (from $80M to $130M). A line-by-line review of the working capital statement shows that inventory is entirely responsible for the increase — it rose $50M (from $25M to $75M, +300%). AR, AP, cash and other items are stable.

math.setup: ROI Year 1 vs Year 3 using Net Profit / Capital Employed
steps: Year 1: ROI = $20M / ($80M PP&E+WC) — exact PP&E split not given, but total capital base is anchored by the $80M working capital figure
Year 3: Capital Employed increased by $50M entirely from inventory
Inventory increase: $75M − $25M = $50M = entire working capital increase
math.answer: Capital Employed grew by $50M driven entirely by a $50M inventory build-up, causing ROI to fall despite higher profits.

questions.prompt: What are the likely root causes of the inventory increase?
questions.guidance: Three main causes: (1) Proliferation of standardized product lines — SKUs grew from 5 to 12, requiring the company to hold finished goods for 12 variants instead of 5; (2) Inaccurate demand forecasts resulting in excess safety stock; (3) Obsolete inventories of outdated product lines that are no longer selling well.

brainstorming.prompt: Management wants to know what it can do to reduce inventory. What options would you recommend?

categories.name: SKU rationalization
ideas: Cut standard product line back to the top 5 products that represent 80% of standard sales
Implement a formal SKU lifecycle review process before adding new variants
Require minimum volume thresholds before launching a new standard product

categories.name: Demand forecasting improvements
ideas: Invest in statistical forecasting tools using historical sell-through data
Implement collaborative forecasting with key retail clients
Review and right-size safety stock levels based on actual demand variability
Set reorder points and safety stock by SKU based on lead time and variability

categories.name: Obsolete inventory management
ideas: Conduct immediate inventory audit to identify slow-moving and obsolete items
Write off or work down obsolete stock (accepts short-term profit hit)
Run promotions or clearance pricing to liquidate slow-moving finished goods
Establish a formal obsolescence reserve policy

categories.name: Process and policy changes
ideas: Adopt a pull-based (build-to-order) approach for slower-moving standard SKUs
Tie inventory performance metrics to management incentives
Implement regular inventory turn reporting to flag issues early

recommendation: Tarrant Fixtures' ROI has fallen over the past three years due to a $50M increase in working capital driven entirely by a 300% increase in finished-goods inventory (from $25M to $75M).

Revenue and profits are healthy — the problem is entirely on the capital side. The root causes are SKU proliferation (standard products grew from 5 to 12), inaccurate demand forecasts creating excess safety stock, and obsolete inventory of discontinued lines.

To restore ROI, the client should: (1) rationalize the standard product line back to the top 5 SKUs representing 80% of standard sales; (2) improve demand forecasting to reduce safety stock to appropriate levels; and (3) write off or work down obsolete inventory.
risks: Writing off obsolete inventory will cause an immediate hit to reported profits, which management may resist.
Cutting the standard product line could disappoint some retail clients who order less common sizes; the client must assess revenue risk before eliminating SKUs.
Improving demand forecasting requires investment in systems and process change.
next_steps: Conduct a detailed inventory audit categorizing stock as active, slow-moving, or obsolete.
Model the ROI impact of reducing inventory back to $25M–$35M range.
Pilot the demand forecasting improvement with the top 5 standard SKUs before rolling out broadly.
Establish a governance process to control future SKU additions in the standard line.
